questions.q: Which four inputs does a rough serving cost estimate primarily depend on?
options: The number of training epochs and the optimizer used
Model size and precision, target context length and concurrency, GPU memory and its hourly cost, and expected (ideally measured) throughput
Only the number of parameters in the model
The size of the pretraining dataset
questions.explain: The estimate needs model size/precision (weight memory), context length/concurrency (KV cache memory), GPU memory and cost, and throughput, which together determine hardware needs and cost per token.

questions.q: In the worked estimate, how is total GPU memory needed calculated?
options: Only the weight memory, ignoring KV cache entirely
Weight memory (params times bytes per param) plus KV cache memory per sequence multiplied by target concurrency
The size of the training dataset divided by batch size
GPU memory needed is fixed regardless of concurrency
questions.explain: Total memory needed is weight_gb (params x bytes_per_param) plus kv_cache_gb_per_seq multiplied by target_concurrency, since every concurrent request needs its own KV cache.

questions.q: Why does the lesson warn against estimating serving throughput from a naive GPU-FLOPs-to-model-FLOPs calculation?
options: Because such calculations always underestimate throughput by exactly half

Because this naive calculation routinely overestimates achievable throughput, since real throughput depends on the actual serving stack, batching strategy, and request-length distribution, not just raw hardware specs
Because GPU FLOPs have nothing to do with inference speed
Because throughput cannot be estimated under any circumstances and must always be guessed
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly states a naive FLOPs-based calculation routinely overestimates achievable throughput, because real-world factors like the serving stack, batching, and request-length distribution matter more than theoretical hardware specs.

questions.q: Why is planning for average load instead of peak load a common mistake in serving cost estimates?
options: Average load estimates are always more accurate than peak load estimates
Because a traffic spike above the average can exceed the provisioned KV cache memory budget, causing the estimate to look fine until real peak demand hits
Peak load never actually occurs in production systems
Concurrency has no effect on memory requirements
questions.explain: KV cache memory scales with concurrency. An estimate based only on average concurrency can look reasonable but fail when real traffic spikes push concurrency, and therefore KV cache memory demand, above what was provisioned.

questions.q: What is the stated purpose of a serving cost estimate like the one in this lesson?
options: To serve as a binding, precise cost quote for a production deployment
To act as a planning tool for deciding whether a model is in a reasonable cost range before committing engineering time, not a substitute for real load testing on the actual stack
To replace the need for any quantization or KV cache analysis
To determine the exact number of GPUs a cloud provider will allocate
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that this estimate is for planning and setting expectations, not a substitute for benchmarking the actual serving stack, on actual hardware, with a realistic request mix.
